name: Chapter 2: Motion in a Straight Line
description: Displacement, velocity, acceleration, x-t and v-t graphs, equations of motion, free fall, relative velocity

cards.term: What is motion?
cards.definition: Change in position of an object with time

cards.term: What is rectilinear motion?
cards.definition: Motion along a straight line

cards.term: What is kinematics?
cards.definition: Describing motion without going into its causes (forces)

cards.term: When can a body be treated as a point object?
cards.definition: When its size is much smaller than the distance it moves in the time considered

cards.term:
Exercise 2.1: which are point objects?
(a) carriage between stations
(b) monkey on a cyclist on a circular track
(c) spinning ball turning sharply
(d) tumbling beaker
cards.definition: (a) and (b). In (c) and (d) the size matters compared with the distance moved

cards.term: Path length vs displacement?
cards.definition: Path length: total distance travelled (scalar, never decreases). Displacement: change in position Δx = x₂ − x₁ (vector, can be 0 or negative)

cards.term: Can displacement be larger than path length?
cards.definition: Never. |displacement| ≤ path length; equal only for motion in one direction without turning back

cards.term: Define average velocity and average speed.
cards.definition: Average velocity = \( \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} \); average speed = total path length ÷ time

cards.term: A man walks 2.5 km to a market in 30 min and returns home in 20 min. Average velocity and average speed for the full 50 min?
cards.definition: Velocity 0 (back home). Speed = 5 km ÷ (5/6 h) = 6 km/h

cards.term: Exercise 2.10(c): the same man, 0 to 40 min (30 min out at 5 km/h, then 10 min back at 7.5 km/h)?
cards.definition: Displacement 1.25 km, path 3.75 km in 2/3 h → average velocity 15/8 km/h, average speed 45/8 km/h

cards.term: Why define average speed as path length ÷ time, not |average velocity|?
cards.definition: Otherwise a tired man who walks to the market and back would have zero average speed

cards.term: Define instantaneous velocity.
cards.definition: \( v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{dx}{dt} \): rate of change of position at that instant

cards.term: How do you read instantaneous velocity from an x–t graph?
cards.definition: Slope of the tangent at that instant

cards.term: Table 2.1 (x = 0.08t³): what happens to Δx/Δt at t = 4 s as Δt shrinks from 2 s to 0.01 s?
cards.definition: It falls 3.92 → 3.86 → 3.845 → … and approaches 3.84 m/s, the instantaneous velocity (= 0.24t²)

cards.term: Example 2.1: x = a + bt² with a = 8.5 m, b = 2.5 m s⁻². Velocity at t = 0 and 2 s?
cards.definition: v = dx/dt = 2bt = 5t: 0 and 10 m/s

cards.term: Example 2.1: average velocity between t = 2 s and 4 s?
cards.definition: [x(4) − x(2)] / 2 = 6b = 15 m/s (the a cancels)

cards.term: For uniform motion, instantaneous vs average velocity?
cards.definition: Equal at every instant

cards.term: What is instantaneous speed?
cards.definition: The magnitude of instantaneous velocity. +24 m/s and −24 m/s both have speed 24 m/s

cards.term: Why is instantaneous speed always equal to |instantaneous velocity|, while average speed can exceed |average velocity|?
cards.definition: Over an infinitesimally small interval the particle cannot turn back, so |displacement| = path length

cards.term: Galileo: is change of velocity constant per unit time or per unit distance in free fall?
cards.definition: Per unit time (constant); per unit distance it decreases. Hence acceleration = rate of change of velocity with time

cards.term: Define average and instantaneous acceleration.
cards.definition: \( \bar a = \dfrac{v_2 - v_1}{t_2 - t_1} \) ; \( a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} \). SI unit m s⁻²

cards.term: How do you read acceleration from a v–t graph?
cards.definition: The slope of the v–t graph (tangent for instantaneous, chord for average)

cards.term: Can acceleration arise without a change in speed?
cards.definition: Yes: a change in direction alone is an acceleration

cards.term: Shape of the x–t graph for a > 0, a < 0 and a = 0?
cards.definition: Curves upward (concave up), curves downward, straight line

cards.term: Fig. 2.3: describe the four v–t graphs.
cards.definition: (a) moving +, speeding up (b) moving +, slowing down (c) moving −, speeding up (d) slows, stops at t₁ and turns back

cards.term: What does the area under a v–t graph give?
cards.definition: The displacement in that time interval

cards.term: How can an area equal a distance?
cards.definition: The axes are velocity [L T⁻¹] and time [T], so "area" has dimensions [L]

cards.term: What does the area under an a–t graph give?
cards.definition: The change in velocity Δv

cards.term: Slopes and areas of motion graphs
cards.definition: Slope of x–t: velocity; Slope of v–t: acceleration; Area under v–t: displacement; Area under a–t: change in velocity; Area under x–t: nothing useful

cards.term: Why can real x–t and v–t graphs not have sharp kinks?
cards.definition: A kink means velocity or acceleration changes instantly; real changes are always continuous

cards.term: Impossible motion graphs (Fig. 2.10)
cards.definition: (a) x–t curve loops back in time: two positions at one instant; (b) v–t circle: two velocities at one instant; (c) speed–t goes below axis: speed cannot be negative; (d) path length–t falls: path length never decreases

cards.term: Identify: which graph cannot describe one-dimensional motion, and why?
cards.definition: All four: two positions or velocities at one time, negative speed, falling path length

cards.term: Exercise 2.13 (Fig. 2.11): does the particle move in a straight line for t < 0 and on a parabola for t > 0?
cards.definition: No: an x–t graph is not the path. Example: a body at rest at x = 0 is dropped at t = 0

cards.term: When is a particle speeding up? Slowing down?
cards.definition: Speeding up: a in the same direction as v. Slowing down: a opposite to v

cards.term: Does a negative acceleration mean slowing down?
cards.definition: No: the sign depends on the chosen axis. A ball falling with "up" positive has a = −g yet speeds up

cards.term: Exercise 2.7(d): must a particle with positive acceleration be speeding up?
cards.definition: No: only if v is also positive. With v < 0, a > 0 means slowing down

cards.term: Exercise 2.7(c): must a particle with constant speed have zero acceleration (1D)?
cards.definition: Yes in 1D: constant speed with no turning means constant velocity. (An instant rebound would need infinite acceleration.)

cards.text: Equations of motion for constant acceleration: {{c1::v = v₀ + at}},  {{c2::x = v₀t + ½at²}},  {{c3::v² = v₀² + 2ax}}.

cards.term: Which quantity is missing from each equation of motion?
How to pick the right equation fast?
cards.definition: Find the one quantity the question neither gives nor asks for, and use the equation without it

cards.term: Average velocity under constant acceleration?
cards.definition: \( \bar v = \dfrac{v_0 + v}{2} \) (true only for constant acceleration)

cards.term: Deriving x = v₀t + ½at² from the v–t area
cards.definition: Rectangle v₀t plus triangle ½(v − v₀)t = ½at²

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Derivation · area of v–t graph

Find the missing step.

Derive x = v₀t + ½at² from the v–t graph of v = v₀ + at.
  1. Area = rectangle + triangle
  2. Rectangle = v₀t
  3. ?
  4. x = v₀t + ½at²
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Derivation · area of v–t graph

Find the missing step.

Derive x = v₀t + ½at² from the v–t graph of v = v₀ + at.
  1. Area = rectangle + triangle
  2. Rectangle = v₀t
  3. Triangle = ½(v − v₀)t = ½(at)t
  4. x = v₀t + ½at²

cards.term: Equations of motion when the particle starts at x₀?
cards.definition: Replace x by (x − x₀): \( x = x_0 + v_0t + \tfrac12 at^2 \), \( v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(x - x_0) \)

cards.term: Deriving v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀) by calculus
cards.definition: Write a = v dv/dx, so v dv = a dx, then integrate

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 2.2 · calculus method

Find the missing step.

Derive v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀) by calculus.
  1. a = dv/dt = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = v dv/dx
  2. ?
  3. Integrate: (v² − v₀²)/2 = a(x − x₀)
  4. v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀)
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 2.2 · calculus method

Find the missing step.

Derive v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀) by calculus.
  1. a = dv/dt = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = v dv/dx
  2. v dv = a dx
  3. Integrate: (v² − v₀²)/2 = a(x − x₀)
  4. v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀)

cards.term: Advantage of the calculus method?
cards.definition: It also works for non-uniform acceleration (a as a function of t, x or v)

cards.term: Are the quantities in the equations of motion scalars?
cards.definition: They are algebraic: put in + or − signs according to the chosen positive direction

cards.term: When are v = dx/dt and a = dv/dt valid vs the equations of motion?
cards.definition: Definitions: always. Equations of motion: only when a is constant in magnitude and direction

cards.term: Teacher addition: distance covered in the nth second?
Teacher addition: a body starts from rest with uniform a. Ratio of distances in the 1st, 2nd, 3rd seconds?
cards.definition: 1 : 3 : 5 (sₙ ∝ 2n − 1)

cards.term: Example 2.3: ball thrown up at 20 m/s from a 25 m high building (g = 10). How high does it rise?
cards.definition: 20 m above the roof (0 = 20² − 2 × 10 × h)

cards.term: Ball from a roof: time to hit the ground
cards.definition: 0 = 25 + 20t − 5t² gives t = 5 s

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 2.3

Find the missing step.

Ball thrown up at 20 m/s from 25 m high roof (g = 10). Time to hit the ground?
  1. Take up +, origin at ground: y₀ = 25, v₀ = 20, a = −10
  2. y = y₀ + v₀t + ½at² with y = 0
  3. ?
  4. t² − 4t − 5 = 0 → (t − 5)(t + 1) = 0 → t = 5 s
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 2.3

Find the missing step.

Ball thrown up at 20 m/s from 25 m high roof (g = 10). Time to hit the ground?
  1. Take up +, origin at ground: y₀ = 25, v₀ = 20, a = −10
  2. y = y₀ + v₀t + ½at² with y = 0
  3. 0 = 25 + 20t − 5t²
  4. t² − 4t − 5 = 0 → (t − 5)(t + 1) = 0 → t = 5 s

cards.term: Why is the single-equation method better in Example 2.3?
cards.definition: Acceleration is constant throughout, so there is no need to split the path at the top

cards.term: Exercise 2.5: 126 km/h car stops in 200 m. Retardation and time?
cards.definition: 3.06 m s⁻² and 11.4 s (v₀ = 35 m/s)

cards.term: Exercise 2.4: a drunkard goes 5 steps forward, 3 back (1 m, 1 s each). Time to fall into a pit 13 m away?
cards.definition: 37 s: 2 m net per 8 s; after 32 s he is at 8 m, then 5 more steps

cards.term: What is free fall?
cards.definition: Motion under gravity alone (air resistance neglected): uniform acceleration g = 9.8 m s⁻² downward

cards.term: Free fall from rest, upward positive: equations?
cards.definition: \( v = -gt, \quad y = -\tfrac12 gt^2, \quad v^2 = -2gy \)

cards.term: a–t, v–t, y–t graphs in free fall (up positive)?
cards.definition: a–t: horizontal line at −g v–t: straight line with slope −g y–t: downward parabola

cards.term: Ball thrown up: velocity and acceleration at the top
cards.definition: At the top v = 0 but a = g downward; velocity shrinks, passes through zero and reverses while a stays constant

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Free fall · intuition

A ball is thrown straight up. At the top, its velocity is zero. Is its acceleration zero there too?

Picture the velocity arrow on the way up and down.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Free fall · intuition

A ball is thrown straight up. At the top, its velocity is zero. Is its acceleration zero there too?

No. a = g downward at every instant, including the top.

If a were 0 at the top, v would stay 0 and the ball would hang in the air. Zero velocity ≠ zero acceleration.

cards.term: Ball thrown up: velocity and acceleration at the highest point?
cards.definition: v = 0, a = g downward (Exercise 2.6)

cards.term: Vertical throw formulas
cards.definition: Maximum height: H = u² / 2g; Time to rise: u / g; Time of flight (back to hand): 2u / g; Speed on return to launch point: u (same as launch)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:

cards.term: Exercise 2.6: ball thrown up at 29.4 m/s (g = 9.8). Height and time to return?
cards.definition: 44.1 m and 6 s

cards.term: Teacher addition: dropped from height h. Time to fall and speed on hitting ground?
cards.definition: \( t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}, \quad v = \sqrt{2gh} \)

cards.term: Trap: a stone is dropped from a balloon rising at 5 m/s. Initial velocity of the stone?
cards.definition: 5 m/s upward (the balloon’s velocity), not zero

cards.term: Galileo's law of odd numbers (free fall)
cards.definition: Distances in successive equal intervals from rest are 1 : 3 : 5 : 7…, because total distance ∝ t² (1, 4, 9, 16…)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Galileo’s law of odd numbers

A stone falls from rest. Distances covered in successive equal time intervals are in what ratio?

Flash a strobe every τ seconds.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Galileo’s law of odd numbers

A stone falls from rest. Distances covered in successive equal time intervals are in what ratio?

1 : 3 : 5 : 7 : 9 …

Positions after τ, 2τ, 3τ… are ∝ 1, 4, 9, 16 (y = ½gt²); the gaps are the differences: 1, 3, 5, 7.

cards.term: Table 2.2: positions after τ, 2τ, 3τ… in units of ½gτ²?
cards.definition: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25… (∝ n²), so gaps are 1, 3, 5, 7, 9

cards.term: Stopping distance of a vehicle braking with deceleration a?
cards.definition: \( d_s = \dfrac{v_0^2}{2a} \) : ∝ square of the speed

cards.term: Double the speed of a car. Stopping distance (same braking)?
cards.definition: 4 times. This is why speed limits in school zones are low

cards.term: What is reaction time?
cards.definition: Time a person takes to observe, think and act

cards.term: Example 2.7: a falling ruler is caught after 21.0 cm. Reaction time?
cards.definition: \( t_r = \sqrt{\dfrac{2d}{g}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 0.21}{9.8}} \approx \) 0.2 s

cards.term: Note: NCERT lists 2.5 Relative velocity, but the rationalised text dropped it. Is it still needed?
cards.definition: Yes: Exercise 2.14 and Chapter 3 use it, and JEE/NEET ask it every year

cards.term: Velocity of B relative to A (1D)?
cards.definition: \( v_{BA} = v_B - v_A \) : velocity of B as seen by an observer moving with A

cards.term: Relative velocity of B with respect to A (same direction)
cards.definition: v_BA = v_B − v_A = 15 − 20 = −5 m/s: B appears to move backward at 5 m/s as seen from A

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Relative velocity · 1D

Car A moves at 20 m/s and car B at 15 m/s, same direction. What is the velocity of B relative to A?

Imagine sitting in car A.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Relative velocity · 1D

Car A moves at 20 m/s and car B at 15 m/s, same direction. What is the velocity of B relative to A?

vBA = vB − vA = 15 − 20 = −5 m/s

From A, B appears to move backward at 5 m/s (and the road rushes back at 20 m/s).

cards.term: Relation between v_AB and v_BA?
Two trains at 54 km/h and 72 km/h approach each other. Relative speed?
cards.definition: 126 km/h = 35 m/s (opposite directions: speeds add)

cards.term: Two bodies with equal velocities: how does each look to the other?
cards.definition: At rest; their separation stays constant and x–t lines are parallel

cards.term: Exercise 2.14: police van at 30 km/h fires a bullet (150 m/s) at a thief’s car at 192 km/h ahead. Speed of impact?
cards.definition: Bullet: 150 + 8.33 = 158.33 m/s car: 53.33 m/s relative 105 m/s

cards.term: Why does the relative speed matter for damage in Exercise 2.14?
cards.definition: The damage depends on how fast the bullet meets the car, i.e. relative to the car

cards.term: Exercise 2.2 (Fig. 2.9): who lives closer, who starts earlier, who walks faster?
cards.definition: A lives closer A starts earlier B walks faster (steeper), overtakes A once

cards.term: Exercise 2.15(a): suggest a situation for this x–t graph.
cards.definition: A ball at rest on a smooth floor is kicked, rebounds from a wall with reduced speed and is stopped by the opposite wall

cards.term: Exercise 2.15(b), (c): situations for the v–t and a–t graphs?
cards.definition: (b) A ball thrown up that rebounds from the floor with less speed each time. (c) A cricket ball moving uniformly, hit back by a bat for a very short time

cards.term: Exercise 2.16 (SHM x–t): signs of x, v, a at t = 0.3 s?
cards.definition: x < 0, v < 0, a > 0. (In SHM, a is always opposite to x)

cards.term: Exercise 2.17 (Fig. 2.14): which interval has the greatest and least average speed?
cards.definition: Greatest in 3 (steepest), least in 2; v > 0 in 1 and 2, v < 0 in 3

cards.term: Exercise 2.18 (Fig. 2.15): acceleration at the points A, B, C, D (speed–time graph)?
cards.definition: Zero at all four: the tangent is horizontal there. |a| greatest in interval 2

cards.term: Chapter 2 traps
cards.definition: Zero velocity means zero acceleration: False (top of a throw); Negative a means slowing down: False (depends on axis); Average speed ≥ |average velocity|: True; Kinematic equations hold for any motion: False (constant a only); Origin and positive direction are a choice: True
